_comment: How to check, by hand, the applicable requirements no automated check can settle and no question in security-notes.json or design-questions.json already asks. One line each, written as an instruction to somebody who is not a programmer: what to go and look at, and what would count as the wrong answer. Nothing here credits anything — the report shows these as still unverified, with the instruction beside them, which is the whole point. A requirement that already has a question in one of the other two catalogs is deliberately absent, and crates/sv-check/tests/human_checks.rs refuses an entry that appears in both.

checks.title: Steps cannot be skipped or done out of order
checks.how: Take a flow with more than one step — checkout, sign-up with a confirmation, anything with a "next" button. Write down the address of the last step. Start the flow again, and go straight to that address without doing the steps before it. It should refuse. Then try the steps in the wrong order, and try the same step twice. Describing the flow in stackvet.toml as `flow` under [stack.run.users] lets `sv report --run` try two skips, one wrong order, and one repeated step for you; other orders, and the last step sent again after the flow finished, are still yours.

checks.title: The live site offers only strong encryption settings
checks.how: `sv` does not check this: it takes dozens of connections to the live site, and `sv probe` keeps to four (the owner's decision, 6 October 2026). Run a scanner made for it against your live address, such as testssl.sh (`testssl.sh https://your-address`) or SSL Labs' free online test. The cipher list should show only ones rated strong or good, with forward secrecy, and no rating of weak, insecure, or vulnerable.

checks.title: The certificate on the live site is one browsers trust
checks.how: Open the live site in a browser and click the padlock. It should show a certificate issued by a public authority, with a date that has not passed, and the name should match the address. A warning page, or a certificate the app generated for itself, means no visitor can tell your site from an impostor.

checks.title: Nothing is past the update deadline you set
checks.how: Write the time frames from your security notes into stackvet.toml as `[policy] fix-within-days`, one number of days per severity, then run `sv report --advisories DIR` (or `sv audit`) against a local advisory database. It lists the packages with a known vulnerability and puts the ones past your time frame first. Those are the answer to this one. Without the numbers it counts every known vulnerability as late, whatever its age.

checks.title: The business limits you wrote down are the ones the app enforces
checks.how: Take each limit from your security notes — so many of something per person, so many per day — and try to go past it in the app. Try it slowly and then quickly, and from two accounts at once if the limit is meant to be global.

checks.title: Two people cannot book the same thing
checks.how: Only where something is limited in number: a seat, a slot, the last item in stock. Open the app in two browsers, get both to the moment of booking the same one, and confirm both as close together as you can. Exactly one should succeed.

checks.title: The banned word list is actually used
checks.how: Take a word from the list you wrote down — the app's name, your organization's name — and try to register an account using it as the password, or with it inside a longer password. It should be refused. Listing the words in stackvet.toml under [policy] as `context-words` lets `sv report --run` try the first one for you, through the app's own sign-up.

checks.title: Passwords from known breaches are refused
checks.how: Try to register with a password known to have been breached. `Password123!` and `qwerty123456` will do; haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords lists more. The app should refuse it and say why, without telling the person anything about other accounts. `sv report --run` tries one such password through the app's own sign-up, but one refusal only supports this: it does not show the whole list is checked.

checks.title: Getting in needs more than a password
checks.how: Sign in and note everything you were asked for. A password alone is a single factor. A code from an app or a security key is a second one. If there is only a password, that is the answer to this one; if you have decided a password alone is enough, ASVS asks for the reasoning to be written down.

checks.title: There is no forgotten way in
checks.how: List every way somebody can become signed in: the password form, any "sign in with" button, magic links by email, API keys, an admin back door, an old mobile app. Compare that with the list in your security notes. Anything not on the list is what this asks about, and each way in should be as strong as the others.

checks.title: Losing a second factor does not become the easy way in
checks.how: Only where people sign in with a second factor. Go through losing it as a person would: what does support ask for before restoring access? If the answer is less than what was asked when the account was set up, the recovery path is now the weakest way in.

checks.title: Being away signs you out
checks.how: Sign in, then leave the app alone for longer than the idle timeout you wrote down, without clicking anything. Come back and reload a private page. You should be asked to sign in again.

checks.title: A session does not last forever
checks.how: Sign in and keep using the app past the maximum lifetime you wrote down. Staying active must not keep it alive forever — at the limit you should be asked to sign in again even mid-use.

checks.title: Secrets live in something built to hold them
checks.how: List where each password, key, and token the app needs actually comes from: a key vault or your host's secret store, an environment variable, or a file in the code. Say who can read each one, and how you would replace one if it leaked. A secret nobody can rotate is the answer to this one.

checks.title: Nothing internal is reachable from outside
checks.how: From a browser that is not signed in, and ideally not on your network, try the addresses that exist for you rather than for visitors: /docs, /swagger, /metrics, /health, /debug, /admin, /.git. Each should either refuse or not exist.

checks.title: You know which of your data is sensitive
checks.how: List every kind of information the app stores, including what it writes to logs and what it keeps in backups. Mark each with how much it would matter if it got out. Anything you cannot place is the thing to look at, and remember that encoded is not the same as protected.

checks.title: Nothing sensitive is handed to an outside service
checks.how: Open the app in a browser with the network panel recording, sign in, and use it normally. Look at every request going somewhere that is not your own address — analytics, error reporting, fonts, chat widgets. Check what is in each, including the address of the page, which often carries names or record numbers. With `browser` under [stack.run.users], `sv report --run` looks through what the signed-in pages send to other sites for the test account's email address, password, and session cookie; but code a page loads from another site cannot run inside the fence, so what analytics and chat widgets send is still yours to look at.

checks.title: Sensitive data is handled the way your notes say
checks.how: Take each protection you wrote down — encrypted, kept for so long, never in logs — and check the app against it. Search the logs for the data that should never appear there, and confirm that something really deletes records when their time is up.

checks.title: Time-consuming features cannot cause a loss of availability
checks.how: Take each time-consuming or resource-demanding feature you documented — an export, a report, an AI request, image processing. Start several at once from one account and see whether the rest of the application stays usable. The defenses you wrote down should stop any one person causing a loss of availability for everybody else.

checks.title: Logs go only where your inventory says
checks.how: Compare the log destinations in your inventory with where they really go: files on the server, your host's logging, any outside service, and anything printed to the console. A destination nobody wrote down is one nobody is watching or protecting.

checks.title: The events you said would be logged really are
checks.how: Do each thing your notes say gets logged — a failed sign-in, a permission refused, a record deleted — then look in the logs and confirm each one is there with enough detail to tell who and when. Then try something that should be refused, such as posting a form with a field the app does not expect, and check that the refusal was logged too.

checks.title: Uploaded files are scanned for viruses
checks.how: Find where a file someone uploads is stored before anyone downloads it, and check whether it is scanned by antivirus software on the way in: your host's upload service may offer this, or a scanner such as ClamAV can be added. Try uploading the harmless EICAR test file, which every antivirus scanner recognizes. If the app accepts it and serves it back, known malicious content would be served too.

checks.title: The app judges how reliable each AI answer is
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you where the app decides how confident it is in an answer the model generated, before showing it. Look for a score or a check, not just the model's text passed straight through. If the answer is shown whatever the model said, the reliability of generated answers is not being assessed.

checks.title: A doubtful AI answer is blocked or replaced
checks.how: With the confidence check from the item above, find the threshold below which an answer is not shown, and what the app shows instead: a fallback message such as "I'm not sure, please contact us". Try asking the AI something it cannot know about your business. It should fall back rather than invent an answer.

checks.title: The AI model has had safety training
checks.how: Look up which model the app uses (your AI coding tool can tell you where it is named) and open the provider's model card or safety documentation. Check that it describes alignment or safety training against disallowed content. Models from the major providers do; a model you downloaded or trained yourself may not, and then this is yours to arrange.

checks.title: The AI's safety is tested again whenever the model changes
checks.how: Write down a short list of prompts the app must refuse or answer carefully, and keep it in version control beside the code. Each time the model is updated or its version changes, run the list again and compare the answers. Check whether this happens today; if nobody reruns anything when the model changes, the answer is no.

checks.title: The AI has been tried against known attacks
checks.how: Try the well-known attacks on the AI part of your app yourself: ask it to ignore its instructions, to reveal its system prompt, to role-play its way past a rule, or hide an instruction inside a document or image it reads. Write down which ones it resisted. A tool such as garak runs many of these adversarial techniques at once.

checks.title: The AI is hardened against tricky inputs
checks.how: Take the attacks from the item above that worked, and check what the app now does about them: input it filters, instructions it keeps apart from what a visitor types, answers it checks before showing. Try each attack again. Hardened means each one that worked before now fails.

checks.title: Someone copying the AI by asking it everything would be noticed
checks.how: Look at what the app records about the questions people ask the AI: who asked, how many, how fast. Check whether anything watches that record for the pattern of someone systematically asking thousands of varied questions to copy what the model knows, the query pattern of an extraction attempt, and warns somebody.

checks.title: Unusual behavior toward the AI is spotted
checks.how: Check whether the app watches for conversations that look like probing: the same question retried many times with small changes, excessive retry attempts, or one visitor trying many different tricks in a row. Try it yourself and look for whether anything was flagged or anyone told.

checks.title: Jailbreak and prompt-injection attempts are recognized
checks.how: List the rules the app uses to recognize attacks aimed at the AI: jailbreak phrasings, prompt injection hidden in documents it reads, attempts to extract its system prompt. Try a few coordinated attempts from two accounts at once, and check whether the rules catch them and something is recorded.

checks.title: A person reviews the code the AI wrote
checks.how: Look at how changes to the app get in: check that every change your AI coding tool wrote is read and approved by a qualified person before it goes live, and that the reviewer is not the same person who asked the AI for the code. The AI agent does not count as the human reviewer. If changes go straight from the AI to the live app, the answer is no.

checks.title: The AI coding tools themselves are attacked on purpose, on a schedule
checks.how: Check whether anyone regularly tries to trick the AI tools that help build the app: a pull request, issue, or comment with a hidden instruction, a known jailbreak, or a request to add a harmful package. Write down when this was last done and what it found, and whether each finding was tracked until fixed. If it has never been done, schedule the first red-team exercise.

checks.title: Input is checked against what the app expects
checks.how: List the places the app takes something typed or sent in that decides what happens next: an amount, a quantity, a date, a status, a role, a choice from a list. For each, try a value it should refuse: a negative or huge number, a date in the past, a word that is not one of the choices, an empty field. The app should refuse it with a message, not accept it and carry on. A form that only checks in the browser does not count: send the same value again with the browser's tools, or ask your AI coding tool to show you the check on the server.

checks.title: Input is cleaned before it reaches a dangerous place
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to list every place the app passes something a person typed into another program: a shell command, a file path, an email header, a spreadsheet export, a search sent elsewhere. For each, look at what it does to the input first. It should allow only the characters that place can safely take, and cut off input that is too long. Then try one: put a semicolon, a quote mark, or a very long line into that field, and check the result is refused or harmless.

checks.title: Text people write cannot run as code in the page
checks.how: If people can write formatted text the app shows to others (Markdown, a comment box, a profile with styling, uploaded stylesheets), try writing a script inside it: a Markdown link to `javascript:alert(1)`, or an HTML `<script>` tag inside the text. Open the page where it is shown, as another user. Nothing should pop up, and the raw tags should be shown as text or removed. If the app takes no formatted text from people, write that down; it does not apply.

checks.title: Directory lookups in Java cannot be steered by input
checks.how: This applies only to an app written in Java or another language that runs on Java. Search the code for `InitialContext`, `lookup(`, and `ldap:`, and check that nothing a person typed reaches the name being looked up. Then check the version of the logging library: Log4j must be 2.17.1 or later, since older versions let a line of text start such a lookup. If the app has no Java in it, write that down; it does not apply.

checks.title: Backup sign-in codes are stored scrambled, not as written
checks.how: If the app gives people backup or recovery codes to sign in with, ask your AI coding tool to show you how they are stored. Open the database (or have the tool show you a row) and look at a stored code. It should be a long scrambled value made by a password hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2, never the code itself. Try signing in with a code the app gave you: it should still work, which shows the scrambled value is checked rather than compared as written.

checks.title: Sign-in codes come from an unpredictable random source
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you the line that makes each sign-in code, reset code, backup code, and two-factor secret. It should use the language's secure random source (`secrets` in Python, `crypto.randomInt` or `crypto.randomBytes` in JavaScript, `SecureRandom` in Java, `crypto/rand` in Go). `random`, `Math.random`, or a code made from the time or the user's id is the wrong answer. `sv check` finds the commonest wrong ones itself; this is for any it did not.

checks.title: One customer's account cannot touch another customer's data
checks.how: This applies when the app keeps separate organizations, teams, or customers apart (tenants). Make two test accounts in two different organizations. Sign in as the first, open something that belongs to it, and write down the address and any id in it. Sign in as the second and try that address, then try changing, deleting, or inviting someone through it. Each should be refused. Do the same with an export or a search, which often skip the check.

checks.title: Keys and signatures are made with approved methods
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to list every place the app makes a key, a signing key, or a signature, and which method each uses. Look for RSA keys of at least 2048 bits (3072 is better), elliptic-curve keys on P-256 or Ed25519, and signatures made with SHA-256 or stronger. MD5, SHA-1, DSA, RSA under 2048 bits, or a key the app writes by hand from random bytes are the wrong answer. If the app makes no keys and signs nothing itself, write that down.

checks.title: Each part of the app can reach only the secrets it needs
checks.how: List where the app's keys and passwords live (a hosting dashboard, a secrets manager, `.env` files, CI settings) and which parts of the app read each one. Check that each service, job, and person has access only to the ones it uses: the website should not hold the payment admin key, a test job should not see production keys, and a database login should not be an administrator unless it must be. `sv check` finds a CI workflow that hands every secret to a job; this covers the rest.

checks.title: Unexpected errors and failed security checks are logged
checks.how: Open the app's logs where they are kept (the hosting dashboard, a log service, or the terminal it runs in). Then cause a few failures: stop the database briefly or give it a wrong password, send a request the app should refuse, and visit an address that makes it fail. Each should leave a line in the log saying what went wrong and when, without a password or key in it. Failures that leave no trace are the wrong answer.

checks.title: Text is put into one standard form before the model reads it
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you what the app does to a person's text before it is sent to the model or turned into an embedding. Look for a step that puts the text into one standard form (Unicode normalization, such as NFKC) so that look-alike characters and invisible ones become plain text. If the text goes straight to the model as typed, that is the wrong answer.

checks.title: Hidden or disguised instructions in input are caught
checks.how: Try sending the AI feature an instruction disguised so a simple filter would miss it: written in Base64, split by invisible characters, in letters from another alphabet that look like English, or inside an HTML comment. Check what the app does. It should refuse, mark the text as untrusted, or strip the disguise before the model sees it, and never follow the hidden instruction.

checks.title: Input that is too long is refused, not cut short
checks.how: Try pasting a very long text into the AI feature, longer than the model can take (several hundred pages of text). The app should refuse it with a message saying it is too long. Cutting it short quietly and carrying on is the wrong answer, because the part cut off can be the part that mattered, such as the instructions at the end.

checks.title: Input to the AI feature is held to the characters it needs
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you the list of characters the AI feature accepts. It should be a list of what is allowed (letters, numbers, ordinary punctuation, the languages your users write in), not a list of what is blocked. Then try sending control characters, emoji sequences, or invisible characters, and check they are refused or removed.

checks.title: Prompts are screened for harmful content before the model
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you where each prompt is checked for violence, self-harm, hate, and sexual content before it reaches the model, and where the limits for each are set. Then try a prompt that clearly crosses one of them (a request for instructions to hurt someone, for example). It should be refused or cleaned, and the limits should be settings you can change, not words written into the code.

checks.title: Content screening works in other languages too
checks.how: Take the harmful prompt you tried for the content screening and translate it into a language your app does not expect, such as one written in a different alphabet. Send it. The app should refuse it or mark it as not screened, rather than let it through because the screening only understood English.

checks.title: Answers built from documents say which documents
checks.how: If the AI feature answers from your own documents or records (retrieval, often called RAG), ask it a question whose answer is in one of them. The answer should name or link the documents it came from. An answer with no sources, or with sources you cannot open, is the wrong answer.

checks.title: The listed sources come from the search, not from the model
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you where the source list under each answer is made. It should come from the records the search actually returned (their titles, ids, or addresses), added by the app. If the model is asked to write its own sources, try asking it to cite a document that does not exist: a made-up source appearing in the list is the wrong answer.

checks.title: Each tool the AI uses has limits on time and resources
checks.how: List the tools the AI feature can use (running code, fetching pages, reading files, querying the database). For each, ask your AI coding tool to show you its limits: how long it may run, how much memory and disk it may use, and where it may connect. Then ask the AI to do something that never ends, such as fetching a page that never answers or running an endless loop. It should be stopped after the limit, not left running.

checks.title: High-impact actions wait for a person to approve them
checks.how: List what the AI feature can do that is hard to undo: sending money, deleting records, emailing customers, changing permissions. Ask it to do each one. The app should stop and ask a person to approve first, and the approval should be checked by the app itself, not just written in the chat. The action going ahead without a click from a person is the wrong answer.

checks.title: The AI's tools run with the least access they need
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool where each tool the AI can use runs, and what it can reach: which files, which database tables, which network addresses, which keys. Each should run in its own sandbox or container with only what it needs (privilege kept to the least). A tool that runs inside the app itself with all its keys and its whole database is the wrong answer.

checks.title: MCP servers come from trusted sources, checked before use
checks.how: List the MCP servers your app or your AI coding tool uses (look in the MCP settings file, such as `.mcp.json`). For each, check where it comes from: the publisher's own registry or repository, at an exact version, with a checksum or signature that is verified when it is installed. A server fetched by name with no version, or downloaded from an unknown site, is the wrong answer. `sv check` flags servers started with no version; this covers where they come from.

checks.title: The MCP server checks every access token fully
checks.how: If your app runs its own MCP server that other tools sign in to, ask your AI coding tool to show you where it checks the access token each request presents. It should check who issued it (issuer), who it is for (audience), that it has not expired (expiration), and what it allows (scope). Then try a token for a different service, an expired one, and one with too little scope: each should be refused.

checks.title: The MCP server does not keep access tokens or passwords
checks.how: If your app runs its own MCP server, ask your AI coding tool to show you everything it stores: database tables, files, logs, caches. Search them for access tokens, refresh tokens, and passwords. The server should check each token and then forget it; finding tokens or user credentials stored anywhere is the wrong answer.

checks.title: Remote MCP connections are encrypted and signed in
checks.how: If your MCP server is reached over the internet, check its address in the settings of the tool that connects to it. It should start with `https://`, and connecting without a token should be refused. Try both: open the address with `http://` in place of `https://`, and connect without signing in. Either one working is the wrong answer.

checks.title: Local-only MCP connections stay on your own computer
checks.how: List the MCP servers set up to run as a local program (the settings show a command to start, rather than an address). Check that each runs only on your own computer or in a controlled environment you set up, never on a shared server that other people or the internet can reach. Anything that needs to be shared should use an encrypted, signed-in connection instead.
